case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a case against Kentucky CHFS social workers, the court held the Fourth Amendment governs a social worker's warrantless in-school interview of a child and requires at least reasonable suspicion of abuse (though that right was not clearly established, so those defendants received qualified immunity), and it affirmed the denial of qualified immunity on the parents' substantive and procedural due-process claims arising from a coerced 'prevention plan' that restricted a mother's unsupervised contact with her children.
key_cases.relevance: This is the governing Sixth Circuit rule for how Kentucky caseworkers may conduct interviews once a report is accepted for investigation.
key_cases.quote: a social worker must have a reasonable suspicion of child abuse before conducting an in-school interview when no other exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement applies

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held there is no child-welfare exception to the Fourth Amendment and that social workers are bound by its warrant requirement when entering a home to investigate abuse, but it reversed the denial of qualified immunity to the social workers because that rule was not clearly established in 2008, while affirming the denial of immunity to the deputy who entered.
key_cases.relevance: This is the binding Sixth Circuit rule that frames what Kentucky investigators may lawfully do at the front door of a home.
key_cases.quote: a social worker, like other state officers, is governed by the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement

key_cases.holding: The Court clarified Kentucky immunity doctrine, holding that public officers and employees sued in their individual capacities enjoy only qualified official immunity, which protects good-faith discretionary acts within the scope of their authority but supplies no protection at all for the negligent performance of ministerial acts; it affirmed immunity for the school board, the athletic director and the KHSAA, and reversed the summary judgments for the two coaches whose duty to enforce a known batting-helmet rule was ministerial.
key_cases.relevance: It draws the ministerial/discretionary line that determines whether a caseworker's handling of an accepted report is protected by qualified official immunity or is actionable in tort.
key_cases.quote: an officer or employee is afforded no immunity from tort liability for the negligent performance of a ministerial act

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that the constitutional right to familial association is circumscribed by the government's interest in protecting children from potential abuse and is not implicated by a governmental investigation into abuse allegations standing alone, and it affirmed dismissal of the parents' § 1983 claims against the social worker and the children's hospital.
key_cases.relevance: This is the principal defense authority once a report is accepted for investigation: opening and conducting an abuse investigation is not itself a constitutional injury to the family.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the right to familial association is not implicated merely by governmental investigation into allegations of child abuse.
